newsitem.title: USA: Anonymous 1943 letter to FBI unmasked Soviet spies.
newsitem.headline: Anonymous 1943 letter to FBI unmasked Soviet spies.

text.p: Key wartime Soviet spies in the United States were unmasked in an anonymous 1943 letter to FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover, U.S. intelligence agencies disclosed on Thursday.

The Russian-language letter, apparently from a disgruntled or disturbed Soviet spy in Washington, accurately fingered General Vasilli Zubilin, then the chief Soviet intelligence officer in the United States; Zubilin's wife, who ran her own network of agents; and other Soviet case officers, including one later recruited by the FBI.

Each was named by the letter's author as an officer of the GPU or NKVD, wartime predecessors of the KGB intelligence and internal security service. Their spy careers have since been documented by decoded intercepts of Soviet intelligence messages.

The undated letter, postmarked Washington, Aug. 7, 1943, was released by the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Security Agency at the start of a two-day on Project "Venona," the allied programme to decipher and exploit Soviet cable traffic collected in the 1940s.

Discussion about the just-disclosed letter to Hoover -- and guessing about the identity of its author -- was to be one highlight of the conference, designed to showcase U.S. spy agencies' steps toward greater openness on materials of chiefly historical interest.

Last year, the National Security Agency, the supersecret Pentagon arm that is the chief U.S. codecracking and communications-intercepting agency, began declassifying and making public all 2,900 of the decrypted "Venona" messages.

The intercepts harvested details about Soviet espionage against the United States, Britain and other World War Two allies, including cover-names for hundreds of Americans, many of them in top government jobs, secretly working for Moscow.

Among the Soviet successes chronicled was the penetration of the ultra-secret Manhattan Project, which developed the atomic bomb used by the United States to end the war against Japan in 1945. Nazi Germany had invaded the Soviet Union and Soviet spies were able to play on sympathy for the Russians in the United States and elswhere.

In formally opening the conference at the National Defence University, Nora Slatkin, the CIA's executive director, portrayed the U.S. bounceback in the late 1940s from sweeping Soviet penetration as a "secret counterattack" based largely on Venona's unlocking of Soviet codes.

"This was a counterattack of persistence, patience, intellect and luck," she said in remarks prepared for delivery. "The Venona revelations not only turned back the Soviet espionage offensive; they spurred us to take badly needed measures to strengthen our own intelligence and counterintelligence effort."

Among the lucky bits referred to by Slatkin may have been the anonymous letter to Hoover, which named as a Soviet spy, among others, Boris Moroz, codename Hollywood, who was turned into a double agent after the war by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and who wrote a book about his spy career.

But the letter to Hoover also contained what historians say was plainly wrong charges that Zubilin, credited in KGB histories with a key role in penetrating the Manhattan Project, and his wife were actually double agents secretly working for Germany and Japan.
"Thus, under cover of the name of the USSR, he (Zubilin) is a dangerous enemy of the USSR and the USA," the letter to Hoover said.

John Haynes, a co-author of the 1995 book "The Secret World of American Communism," attributed the apparent smear in the letter to a Soviet intelligence officer "who was either extremely angry at Zubilin or who wanted to cause him a lot of trouble or some combination of those things."
